```{r decisions-setup, include=FALSE}
has_gmp <- requireNamespace("gmp", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_gmp, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%")
options(width = 90)
library(postrank)
```

A multidomain report assigns each unit one grade in each domain. Smaller
grade labels mean higher reported priority within that domain. A tie
withholds a direction; it does not assert that the latent targets are equal.
This article explains when separate domain choices solve the reporting
problem, and when the dependence between domains changes the chosen profile.
The executable examples use small, independently specified synthetic inputs,
run offline, and need no optimization backend. The exact and MCMC examples
run when the suggested package `gmp` is installed.

## Additive loss and separate choices

Let $G_d$ be the grade column in domain $d$, $F_d$ the number of false
disclosed directions in a posterior state, and $T_d$ the number of withheld
pairs. A strict direction at latent equality is false. With $n$ original
units, $M = {n \choose 2}$ remains the loss denominator, even when a card
withholds some comparisons. The additive expected loss is

\[
R(G) = \sum_d w_d\{E(F_d) + \tau_d T_d\}/M.
\]

Its domain terms depend only on the corresponding marginal law. Suppose the
declared family is a Cartesian product of domain banks and every constraint
is domain specific, such as structural equality, grade caps, or an
expected-error guard. The feasible family is then also a Cartesian product.
Minimizing each weighted domain term separately minimizes the sum; combining
the complete sets of those minimizers gives every minimum in that product.
For a zero-weight domain, every feasible column minimizes its weighted term.
This conclusion does not require independent
posterior domains. A common-grade requirement or another constraint linking
columns would require a different argument.

A joint protection requirement changes the feasible set. For example, write
$N_d$ for the number of disclosed pairs in the specified scope and require

\[
J(G) = P\{\text{at least one }d\text{ has }F_d > t_d N_d\}
\leq \alpha.
\]

This is a union within the **same posterior state**. Dependence can change
its probability while leaving the marginal errors and additive loss
unchanged. If $N_d=0$, that domain's exceedance event is structurally false;
the corresponding error fraction is undefined rather than a measured zero.

## Two units, two domains, unchanged marginal errors

Units A and B have binary priority values. In a normal state A is above B
in both domains. A reversal exchanges their values. The two complete finite
laws below differ only in how their reversals occur together:

| Law | Normal in both | Reverse domain one only | Reverse domain two only | Reverse both |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Coincident | 9/10 | 0 | 0 | 1/10 |
| Disjoint | 8/10 | 1/10 | 1/10 | 0 |

In either domain of either law, reporting A above B has error probability
1/10. Set equal domain weights, tie loss `tau = "1/4"`, strict threshold
`t = "0"`, and joint cap `alpha = "3/20"`. Character fractions preserve
these exact policy values.

```{r decisions-finite-inputs}
units <- c("A", "B")
domains <- c("one", "two")
targets <- setNames(lapply(domains, function(d) list(
  definition = paste("Fictional priority in domain", d),
  units = "arbitrary priority units", orientation = "larger_is_higher",
  equality_classes = units,
  equality_provenance = "A and B are distinct modeled targets.")), domains)

# Each row specifies the reversals in one complete joint state.
make_states <- function(reverse, ids) {
  x <- array(0, c(nrow(reverse), 2L, 2L),
    dimnames = list(ids, units, domains))
  for (d in seq_along(domains)) {
    x[, "A", d] <- ifelse(reverse[, d], 1, 2)
    x[, "B", d] <- ifelse(reverse[, d], 2, 1)
  }
  x
}
make_law <- function(id, reverse, masses) {
  postrank_mdomain_input(
    make_states(reverse, paste0(id, "-", seq_len(nrow(reverse)))),
    targets = targets,
    provenance = list(input_id = id, law_id = id, proper_law = TRUE,
      joint_generation = "Complete finite support authored in this article.",
      sampling_assumptions = list(
        finite_support_origin = "All support states and exact masses listed here.")),
    representation = "exact_finite_law", masses = masses)
}
laws <- list(
  coincident = make_law("coincident",
    rbind(c(FALSE, FALSE), c(TRUE, TRUE)), c("9/10", "1/10")),
  disjoint = make_law("disjoint",
    rbind(c(FALSE, FALSE), c(TRUE, FALSE), c(FALSE, TRUE)),
    c("8/10", "1/10", "1/10")))
policy <- postrank_mdomain_decision(tau = "1/4", t = "0", alpha = "3/20")
```

Declare three columns per domain: withhold, A above B, and B above A.
Their full Cartesian product has nine candidates. No direction is omitted
from this stated bank. The optimum claims below concern this bank.

```{r decisions-full-bank}
columns <- list(withhold = c(A = 1L, B = 1L),
  A_above_B = c(A = 1L, B = 2L), B_above_A = c(A = 2L, B = 1L))
families <- lapply(laws, postrank_mdomain_family,
  columns = list(one = columns, two = columns), max_actions = 9L)
fits <- lapply(names(laws), function(id)
  postrank_mdomain_solve(laws[[id]], families[[id]], policy, max_actions = 9L))
names(fits) <- names(laws)

column_label <- function(g) {
  if (g[1L] == g[2L]) "withhold" else
    if (g[1L] < g[2L]) "A above B" else "B above A"
}
candidate_display <- function(fit) {
  tab <- fit$candidate_table
  actions <- fit$solution$actions[tab$action_id]
  data.frame(
    one = vapply(actions, function(g) column_label(g[, "one"]), ""),
    two = vapply(actions, function(g) column_label(g[, "two"]), ""),
    risk = tab$risk_exact, joint_probability = tab$J_exact,
    feasible = tab$feasible_for_represented_measure, optimal = tab$optimal,
    row.names = NULL)
}
knitr::kable(candidate_display(fits$coincident),
  caption = "All nine candidates: coincident reversals")
knitr::kable(candidate_display(fits$disjoint),
  caption = "All nine candidates: disjoint reversals")
```

The dual report A above B has expected loss 1/10 under either law. Its joint
error probability is 1/10 for coincident reversals and 1/5 for disjoint
reversals. Thus it passes the 3/20 cap only under the coincident law.
The disjoint law has two tied optima: report A above B in either one domain
and withhold the other. Each has loss
$(1/2)(1/10 + 1/4) = 7/40$ and joint probability 1/10.

```{r decisions-fixed-dual}
dual <- matrix(c(1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), 2L,
  dimnames = list(units, domains))
dual_evaluations <- lapply(laws, postrank_mdomain_evaluate,
  grades = dual, decision = policy)
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(laws), function(id) {
  e <- dual_evaluations[[id]]
  data.frame(law = id, error_one = e$domain_table$EF_exact[1L],
    error_two = e$domain_table$EF_exact[2L], risk = e$risk_exact,
    joint_probability = e$J_exact,
    feasible = e$feasible_for_represented_measure)
})), caption = "The same dual card under the two joint laws")
stopifnot(all(vapply(dual_evaluations,
  function(e) all(e$domain_table$EF_exact == "1/10"), TRUE)))
```

```{r decisions-all-optima}
optima <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(id) {
  fit <- fits[[id]]
  tab <- candidate_display(fit)
  data.frame(law = id, tab[tab$optimal, ], row.names = NULL)
}))
knitr::kable(optima, caption = "The complete optimizer sets in the declared banks")
stopifnot(fits$coincident$optimizer_count == 1L,
  fits$disjoint$optimizer_count == 2L,
  fits$coincident$evaluation$risk_exact == "1/10",
  fits$disjoint$evaluation$risk_exact == "7/40",
  all(vapply(fits, function(f) f$search_scope$examined_actions == 9L, TRUE)))
```

Disabling joint protection recovers the separate-choice result: the dual
report is optimal for both laws. Marginal expected errors and expected loss
did not change; the union constraint is what coupled the feasible choices.
An arbitrary pairing or permutation of separate marginal draws cannot
establish which joint law applies.

```{r decisions-separable}
separable_policy <- postrank_mdomain_decision(tau = "1/4", t = NULL)
separate_fits <- lapply(names(laws), function(id)
  postrank_mdomain_solve(laws[[id]], families[[id]], separable_policy,
    max_actions = 9L))
knitr::kable(data.frame(law = names(laws),
  optimum_risk = vapply(separate_fits, function(f) f$evaluation$risk_exact, ""),
  optimizer_count = vapply(separate_fits, `[[`, 1L, "optimizer_count")))
stopifnot(all(vapply(separate_fits,
  function(f) identical(unname(f$grades), matrix(c(1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), 2L)), TRUE)))
```

## Reading a frozen 40-site illustration

The installed JSON below is a small, frozen output illustration for 40
fictional sites from JoonHo Lee's
[Need-Based Prekindergarten Funding tutorial](https://github.com/joonho112/need-based-prek-funding-tutorial).
Domain S describes student-composition economic need and domain C describes
catchment-community economic need; both use larger values for higher need.
These are distinct target definitions, including conditional predictive S
targets for new sites. Sharing a community target does not identify student
targets: S05/S06 and S21/S22 are declared C identity pairs, while all 40 S
targets are distinct. The original all-pair denominator is 780.

The original calculation used 8,000 retained states from chains 1–2 for
selection, a declared seven-column bank per domain (49 candidate cards),
and a fixed-card diagnostic replay on 8,000 states from chains 3–4. Ordering
the candidate columns used the selection states. The two cases share equal
weights, `tau = "1/10"`, `q = "1/20"` and `alpha = "1/20"`; the wide case
changes `t` from 5% to 10%. Their distinct case IDs preserve that difference.

**This vignette reads the frozen grades and summary counts. It does not run
the original 40-site analysis, load its posterior archive, select a new card,
or perform a new validation.** The public
[reproducibility appendix](https://github.com/joonho112/need-based-prek-funding-tutorial/blob/ff223082b27c8af92f762c20f49092f06b19a913/appendices/D-reproducibility.qmd)
describes the external tutorial workflow. Source commit, relative input path,
hash and changes are recorded in the JSON; none is an installation-time
dependency. Reproducing the multidomain analysis separately requires the
original identified joint states, target/equality map, chain allocation and
the stated 7-by-7 candidate design, rather than these summaries alone.

```{r decisions-frozen-card, eval=TRUE}
frozen <- jsonlite::read_json(system.file("extdata", "mdomain",
  "synthetic40-card.json", package = "postrank"), simplifyVector = TRUE)
knitr::kable(frozen$cases[, c("case_id", "t", "N_S", "N_C", "risk_exact",
  "selection_J_exact", "diagnostic_J_exact")],
  caption = "Stored results; rational values refer to the supplied empirical measures")
```

The primary card withholds every S comparison and discloses 500 C
comparisons in grades of size 10, 10 and 20. Its selection risk is
170039/2496000. Strict 5% exceedance among 500 disclosed pairs requires at
least 26 errors; exactly 25 does not exceed the threshold. No selection
state exceeded the threshold, although 1,871 had at least one error. Hence
`J = 0` describes zero observed exceedances at that threshold, and does not
say that the card made no errors.

The wide card discloses 300 S pairs and 500 C pairs. Its selection risk is
716341/12480000 and its selection exceedance rate is 266/8000 = 133/4000.
The same fixed card gives 229/8000 in the diagnostic chains. Exact fractions
here mean exact arithmetic for the represented equal-weight empirical
measure. Splitting chains and recording disjoint state IDs does not establish
independence or an iid numerical certificate for the intended posterior.

```{r decisions-frozen-grades, eval=TRUE}
knitr::kable(frozen$grades,
  caption = "Frozen grades: smaller numbers indicate higher priority within each domain")
wide_grades <- as.matrix(frozen$grades[, c("wide_S", "wide_C")])
rownames(wide_grades) <- frozen$grades$unit_id
colnames(wide_grades) <- c("S", "C")
occupancy <- table(C = factor(wide_grades[, "C"], levels = 1:3),
                   S = factor(wide_grades[, "S"], levels = 1:2))
knitr::kable(occupancy, caption = "Wide card: rows are C grades, columns are S grades")
knitr::kable(wide_grades[c("S11", "S18"), , drop = FALSE],
  caption = "A crossed pair: S11 has higher S priority; S18 has higher C priority")
```

The occupancy rows are (6, 4), (4, 6), and (0, 20): five of six profile
cells are occupied. Of 548 unique pairs disclosed in at least one domain,
16 have opposite directions across domains. S11=(1,2) and S18=(2,1) are
one such pair. There is no single best ordering of these two sites implied
by this profile; an application would need an additional decision rule to
collapse the two domain priorities.

The derived JSON credits JoonHo Lee and preserves the original artificial
values' [CC BY 4.0 terms](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
It retains only fictional IDs, selected grade columns, aggregate counts and
source identity. No raw posterior states, geographic layers, school records
or catchment database are bundled. Original tutorial code is separately MIT
licensed; the source-specific exclusions remain in its
[rights notice](https://github.com/joonho112/need-based-prek-funding-tutorial/blob/ff223082b27c8af92f762c20f49092f06b19a913/RIGHTS.md).

## Inspecting MCMC history for a fixed report

The following independent, tiny synthetic example demonstrates the MCMC
assessment API. It generates two short Markov histories of unequal lengths.
The two-state transition probabilities are 1/10 from normal to reversed and
2/5 in reverse; the stationary reversal probability is 1/5. A whole state
reverses both domains together. Original chain order and iteration numbers
are retained. These short histories illustrate diagnostic fields, not a
recommended simulation length or evidence about the 40-site source.

```{r decisions-mcmc}
simulate_chain <- function(n) {
  z <- logical(n)
  z[1L] <- stats::runif(1) < 1/5
  for (i in 2:n)
    z[i] <- if (z[i - 1L]) stats::runif(1) >= 2/5 else stats::runif(1) < 1/10
  z
}
set.seed(1202)
chains <- list(chain_A = simulate_chain(24L), chain_B = simulate_chain(31L))
z <- unlist(chains, use.names = FALSE)
history <- data.frame(source_index = seq_along(z),
  chain_id = rep(names(chains), lengths(chains)),
  iteration_id = unlist(lapply(chains, seq_along), use.names = FALSE))
history_input <- postrank_mdomain_input(
  make_states(cbind(z, z), paste0("markov-", seq_along(z))), targets = targets,
  provenance = list(input_id = "tiny-markov-history", law_id = "tiny-markov-law",
    proper_law = TRUE,
    joint_generation = "Both domains use the same synthetic binary chain state.",
    retention = list(warmup_removed = 0L, thinning = 1L),
    sampling_assumptions = list(sampler = "Two-state Markov transition simulator.",
      chain_details = "Lengths 24 and 31; stationary initial draws; seed 1202.",
      target_assertion = "Stationary reversal probability 1/5 by the specified transitions.")),
  representation = "mcmc_equal_weight_draws", state_origin = history)
fixed_grades <- matrix(c(1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), 2L,
  dimnames = list(units, domains))
assessment <- postrank_mdomain_assess(history_input, fixed_grades, policy,
  method = "mcmc", batch_size = 10L,
  design = list(role = "synthetic_method_demonstration"))
chain_table <- assessment$native$chain_table
knitr::kable(chain_table[chain_table$event_id == "joint-union",
  c("chain_id", "n_retained", "hit_count", "rate", "max_zero_run",
    "partial_batch_count")], digits = 3)
batch_table <- assessment$native$batch_table
knitr::kable(batch_table[batch_table$event_id == "joint-union" & batch_table$partial,
  c("chain_id", "batch_id", "n_retained", "hit_count", "rate", "partial")],
  caption = "Final partial batches remain in the diagnostic record", digits = 3)
assessment$assurance[c("certificate_basis", "numerical_guarantee",
  "convergence_established", "independence_established")]
stopifnot(!assessment$joint_certificate,
  !assessment$assurance$numerical_guarantee,
  identical(assessment$native$histories$chain_id, history$chain_id))
```

Use hit counts, long zero runs and batch-to-batch variation to inspect how
well a run has explored the event relevant to the fixed report. A zero-hit
history is different from a structurally impossible event. Unequal chain
rates must be combined using their retained state counts; a simple average
of their rates changes the empirical measure. Batch rates are descriptive
and are not independent replicates. This route does not supply an iid
binomial certificate, a convergence proof, or a held-out interpretation.
See `?postrank_mdomain_assess` for the separate fixed-sample iid route and
its required design record, and `vignette("mdomain-quickstart")` for the
input-to-report workflow.
